summary.text: The photoelectric effect is the release of electrons from a material when light, such as ultraviolet, shines on it.
Experiments showed electrons come out only when the light is above a certain frequency, however bright it is or however long it shines, which classical wave theory could not explain.
Einstein explained it by treating light as discrete energy packets, and the effect helped shape the idea of wave-particle duality.

facts.label: Emitted electrons
facts.value: Electrons knocked out this way are called photoelectrons

facts.label: Frequency threshold
facts.value: Electrons leave only above a certain light frequency

facts.label: Photon energy
facts.value: A photon's energy is proportional to the light's frequency

facts.label: Typical energy needed
facts.value: Metals need a few electron-volts, from short-wavelength visible or ultraviolet light

facts.label: Practical use
facts.value: Used in devices that detect light and time electron emission

items.prompt: You shine a very bright red lamp on a metal and no electrons come out. A friend says to make it ten times brighter. Will that help?

options.label: Yes, more brightness will eventually build up enough energy
No, brightness alone does not help if the frequency is too low
Yes, but only if you wait much longer under the light
No, because metals never release electrons to any light

items.explain: Electrons are dislodged only above a certain frequency, regardless of intensity or exposure time. More low-energy photons never add up to one big enough photon.

items.prompt: Classical wave theory predicted very dim light would simply cause a delay before electrons were emitted. What did experiments show?

options.label: Emission happened only after the light had built up energy
Dim light and bright light gave exactly the same results
Emission depended on frequency, not on intensity or exposure time
Emission got stronger the longer the light stayed on

items.explain: The results disagreed with the classical prediction: electrons are dislodged only above a certain frequency, regardless of intensity or duration.

items.prompt: Two beams have the same frequency, but one is three times as intense. How do the emitted electrons compare in energy?

options.label: The brighter beam gives each electron three times the energy
The dimmer beam gives each electron more energy
Both beams give the electrons the same energy
Neither beam can release any electrons at all

items.explain: The energy of emitted electrons depends only on the energy of the individual photons, not on the intensity of light of a given frequency.

items.prompt: An electron absorbs a photon and escapes. Where does the photon's energy go?

options.label: All of it goes into the electron's motion after escape
Part frees the electron, and the rest becomes its motion
Half is kept by the light beam and half goes to the electron
All of it goes into freeing the electron, leaving it motionless

items.explain: Part of the energy liberates the electron from its binding and the rest contributes to its kinetic energy.

items.prompt: Why do most photoelectric experiments use clean metal surfaces inside evacuated tubes?

options.label: Oxide layers raise the energy barrier, and vacuum keeps gases from blocking the flow
Metals only conduct when sealed away from every kind of light
Clean surfaces create the light that frees the electrons
Vacuum makes photons heavier so they eject more electrons

items.explain: Nonconductive oxide layers increase the barrier to photoemission, and a vacuum stops gases from impeding the electrons between electrodes.

items.prompt: Why did the photoelectric effect matter for the bigger picture of physics?

options.label: It proved that light is purely a continuous wave
It showed electrons cannot be moved by any light
It replaced the need for metals in electronics
It revealed light's quantum nature and fed into wave-particle duality

items.explain: Studying the effect led to key steps in understanding the quantum nature of light and electrons and influenced wave-particle duality.
